overview: The first scan nominates samples for several independent visual reasons and leaves all original times accessible. A second pass compares anchors on each side of a candidate transition and flags intervals worth investigating. Cumulative measured change is a separate coordinate from time; close sample spacing in seconds can still leave a change gap. The AMR tree records how a coarse interval was subdivided in time or into image regions, with parent and sibling context. The catalogue and wave give starting points. Original pictures obtained through delivery_request or source_resample are the visual evidence. Use the receipt ID to check the source and scope with evidence_reference or claim_verify. A branch depth or an automatic stop records processing state only; hidden content and physical continuity remain unknown.
examples: For repeated changes whose location is unknown, amr_query({start:0,end:2,page_size:4}) lists candidate intervals. Replace the illustrative bounds with any valid source seconds and read a returned node_id: amr_query({node_id:"source",detail:"wave"}) retrieves the underlying wave and amr_query({node_id:"source",detail:"links"}) retrieves saved evidence. If the two ends leave a useful gap, amr_refine({node_id:"source",mode:"time",reason:"Compare the original samples between the endpoints"}) obtains a verified interior sample and records children. With two actual PTS inside a node, a native pixel rectangle can be supplied with mode:"space", pts:[...], native_xywh:[x,y,width,height], and an optional crop_pts equal to one supplied PTS. Read evidence_detail with a returned result_ref to check applicability and the source; geometric matching does not prove identity. For a clear event at a known time, source_resample with your preferred density is sufficient. If a node ID fails, query by time and use a returned ID. Use exact integer source PTS rather than seconds for frame and crop requests.
advantages: An ordinary range reread is the straightforward choice when you already know where to look or need evenly spaced originals. AMR is most useful when visually similar events recur, when you want to recover a saved comparison at a smaller scale without guessing a new time window, or when your current endpoint views leave an unresolved local detail. It groups saved comparisons, parent/child ranges, and accessible source images in one place; it does not make every moment important. Use a flat list for scanning unrelated regions, waveform for coarse activity, and the hierarchy for narrowing or revisiting a branch. Use only the tools that help your question and stop when the evidence warrants.
